frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d262:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 record an evening session at half past nine. Ambassador Harriman briefed the chiefs on the Soviet attitude ahead of the Tehran meeting. General Marshall had asked him to speak to the proposals of the Joint Strategic Survey Committee.

Harriman expects no detailed Soviet strategy plan, since Moscow is wholly absorbed in its own fighting, and he warns against arriving with a cut-and-dried plan of their own. The Soviets hate being handed finished decisions, he says, but frank explanation has worked well, and Stalin has already told his people a second front is coming soon. Harriman also reports strong Soviet pressure to end the war fast, and a firm intent to join the war on Japan once Germany falls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d362:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the dinner conversation at Tehran on 28 November 1943, beginning at half past eight in the evening. After talk of where the leaders might meet next, with Fairbanks in Alaska favored, Stalin opens the question of France's future.

Stalin argues at length that France's ruling class is rotten to the core. It delivered the country to Germany. It deserves neither gentle treatment nor her empire back, since no strategic points can safely be left in French hands. Roosevelt partly agrees, naming New Caledonia and Dakar as points needing trusteeship or firm control. Churchill answers that the four victorious nations must hold the world's strategic points. On Germany, Roosevelt wants the very word Reich struck out; Stalin replies that the Reich itself must be made impotent, and presses for stronger measures than either Western leader names.

Officers sent abroad on temporary duty reported what they learned in memoranda like this one, which could travel further than a cable. London in April 1944 was the headquarters of the coming invasion and a listening post for all Europe. For readers, Matthews's paper shows a professional diplomat gathering impressions at the center of the war, weeks before D-Day changed every calculation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d62: Harry Hopkins wrote to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on October 26, 1943, and the message is Document 62 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hopkins, the President's special assistant, was the channel Roosevelt trusted most, and his letters carried weight beyond their rank. The record names the writer, the receiver, and the date. It sits in the Foreign Relations series among the papers of the Moscow Conference's final days.
frus-1944-quebec-d162:
The United States Chiefs of Staff answered the British Pacific proposals on September 8, 1944, in C.C.S. 452/25. The paper is only a few lines long, but it settles a large question. London's preferred option, a British fleet under American command in the main operations, was not the one Washington accepted here.

Instead the Americans accepted the alternative: a British Empire task force under a British commander, built from British, Australian, and New Zealand land, sea, and air forces. It would operate in the Southwest Pacific under General MacArthur's supreme command. The chiefs noted this would still place the British Fleet well to reinforce the American Pacific Fleet if later desired.
frus-1944-quebec-d262:
A secretaries' note, C.C.S. 417/9 of September 11, 1944, records the Combined Chiefs' informal acceptance of a new statement of the over-all objective against Japan. The restatement replaced the older formula in C.C.S. 417/2. It was accepted subject to the assurances the British had requested and the Americans had given in the preceding papers of the series.

The objective was to force Japan's unconditional surrender in two ways. First, lower her ability and will to resist by sea and air blockade, intensive bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength. Second, invade and seize objectives in her industrial heart. Marshall had explained the new wording was designed to allow for invasion of the home islands.
frus-1944-quebec-d62:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff prepared this memorandum on September 10, 1944, two days before the Quebec Conference opened. The British mission in Washington worked alongside the American chiefs year-round. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

A staff paper dated on the conference's eve usually fixes a delegation's final positions. The British chiefs' representatives in Washington coordinated with London and with the traveling British party at Quebec. For readers, the memorandum shows both staffs converging on Canada with their arguments in order, ready for the sessions that would settle the war's last campaigns.
frus-1945-50-intel-d162:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 13 August 1946. The State Department prints it as document 162 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d262:
Dated 26 March 1948, this memorandum runs from Secretary of Defense Forrestal to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The State Department prints it as document 262 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d362:
Dated 8 February 1949, this letter runs from Allen W. Dulles to Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense. It is document 362 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Letters like this one let a reader follow a debate between two offices in their own words. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d62: A memorandum for the record, dated 27 December 1945, was written to fix an event or a talk in writing before memory faded. Officers wrote such notes to protect the file and themselves. This one falls in the last week of 1945. The long argument over a central intelligence system was nearly settled, and the January directive was being readied. Its bare title names no author and no reader, so it stands as a small act of record-keeping inside a famous negotiation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d162:
Churchill answered Roosevelt on Poland on 6 January 1945, in his message number 876. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He thanks the President for Stalin's reply and remarks drily on the new actor in the story, the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet.

Britain, Churchill reports, has made its stand plain, in parliament among other places: it continues to recognize the London Poles as the government of Poland. His own fresh note to Stalin calls the course of events distressing. Much the best thing, he told Stalin, is for the three leaders to meet and talk these matters through. The whole world picture, war and the passage to peace alike, should frame the talk. Meanwhile the British attitude stays unchanged.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d262:
General Leslie Groves reported the state of the atomic bomb to General Marshall on 30 December 1944. His top secret letter from the War Department, headed “Atomic Fission Bombs,” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Groves ran the Manhattan District project that built the weapon.

Planning, he writes, should rest on the gun-type bomb, expected to equal ten thousand tons of TNT. The first bomb should be ready about 1 August 1945, with no full-scale test thought necessary beforehand. A second should follow by the end of the year. Hopes for the implosion type by late spring have faded on scientific difficulties not yet solved. Material for a first implosion bomb should exist by late July, with a much smaller yield at first.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d362:
Caring for freed prisoners brought Eden to write to Molotov at Yalta on February 5, 1945. He recalled their Moscow talks of the past October on repatriation. Soviet citizens freed in the south and west, and British subjects freed in the east, all needed food, shelter, and a way home. Drafts had passed between the governments since then.

A Soviet redraft had reached the British Embassy on January 20. London had studied it, Eden wrote, and found it generally acceptable, with points stated below. A like draft had gone to Washington. Because the Allied commands were joined, Eden argued, the answer should be joined too.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d462: Oil slipped into the last Yalta lunch, and Bohlen's short note of February 11, 1945, preserves the moment. The three leaders, their foreign secretaries, ambassadors, and interpreters ate together, and talk stayed general and personal. Then Stalin made an obvious reference to Iran. Any nation, he said, which kept its oil in the ground and would not let it be used was in fact working against peace. The remark aimed at Persia's stalled concessions, and perhaps further. It reads like a preview of the oil politics ahead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d62:
No reporters would cover the Big Three meeting if Churchill got his way. In a personal and top secret telegram of 21 January 1945, he put the idea to President Roosevelt. The message, numbered 891, is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Churchill proposes barring the press from the conference, code-named Argonaut, entirely. Each leader could still bring three or four uniformed service photographers. Their still and motion pictures would be released only when the leaders chose. He also expects the usual agreed communiqué at the end. A matching telegram went to Stalin, and Roosevelt's agreement followed the next day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d162:
Secretary Stettinius suggested a council of foreign ministers in a telegram from San Francisco dated June 19, 1945. The extract is document 162 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers the President's June 9 request for ideas on how the European peace settlements should be worked out.

A full-dress peace conference should be avoided, Stettinius argues. The problems should instead be handled case by case by a council of foreign ministers. The idea could be sounded out with the British first, and the Russians told that Washington meant to raise it at the Big Three meeting. There the leaders would try to fix the new council's first meeting, its time and place, and some of its agenda. The proposal became the Council of Foreign Ministers created at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d262:
Naval aide George Elsey reported another blank in the files in an undated note printed as document 262 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Like its companion on the rivers, it was submitted to Admiral Leahy on July 1, 1945, and forwarded to the President.

There has been no reference, Elsey writes, to the free use of the Suez and Panama canals in either president's Map Room papers. The Kiel Canal is a different story. Churchill reported to Roosevelt after his Moscow talks of October 1944 that Stalin wanted the Kiel Canal internationalized, and that Churchill agreed with him. No details were given, the subject was not discussed at Yalta, and it has not been mentioned since. The note left Truman free to shape his own line on the canals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d362: Pauley assured President Truman from Moscow on June 29, 1945, that a plan was coming. He was bending every effort, he wrote, to have a proposed reparations plan ready. It would go to Truman and to the heads of the British and Soviet governments at their forthcoming meeting. Only an extract of his top secret cable is printed here. Its substance stays in the fuller version printed elsewhere in the volume. The note went to the Secretary of State ad interim over Ambassador Harriman's signature.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d462:
Reuters comes under fire in an extract from Shantz's Belgrade telegram of July 11, 1945. The Yugoslav paper Borba sharply criticized the news agency for protectionism toward the Greeks in the Yugoslav-Greek dispute over the treatment of Macedonians in northern Greece. Its editorialist denied a Reuters charge that Yugoslavia wished to make territorial claims on Greece.

He pointed instead to the alleged expansionist ambitions of Greek chauvinist officials. He admitted that Yugoslavs, and all true democrats, stand against the Athens government. Yugoslavia, he said, hopes the question of Greek misrule in Macedonia will come before an international forum, if not the Big Three conference itself. The extract preserves Belgrade's case in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d562:
Marshal Stalin sent President Truman a personal and secret letter on June 21, 1945. It is document 562 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The letter, sent from Moscow in translation, protests Allied handling of the Trieste and Istria dispute.

Stalin says Yugoslavia had met the Allies halfway by taking their proposal. Yet talks in Trieste had hit a dead end, since Allied officers would not weigh even small Yugoslav points. He attacks Field Marshal Alexander's tone and his public words likening Tito to Hitler and Mussolini. He also calls the June 2 Anglo-U.S. note an ultimatum in tone. He closes by hoping that just Yugoslav claims will be met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d62:
Churchill gave the Potsdam Conference its code name in telegram number 89 to President Truman, sent from London on June 15, 1945. The one-line message is document 62 in the Foreign Relations papers on the conference. A code word let officials talk about the secret Berlin meeting without naming it in cables and files.

Churchill suggests the word Terminal for the coming conference and asks if Truman agrees. A note in the volume adds that he made the same proposal to Stalin the same day, and Stalin also said yes. The name fit the moment: Berlin was meant to be the last stop of the wartime alliance's grand strategy, the terminal point of the road through Tehran and Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d662:
Paris ambassador Caffery reported Moscow's Tangier note to the French on July 2, 1945. His secret wire is document 662 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Russian note answered the notification delivered in Moscow on June 30.

The note expressed astonishment that the talks were called with so little notice to Moscow. It stated Russian interest in Tangier and asked that the opening be put off. Consultations should first arrange four-power discussions. A French official, Meyrier, told British colleagues the Russian move was inevitable. London and Washington wanted a temporary regime in place of Spain's, while France wanted the 1939 state of things restored. If the French plan were adopted, he said, the Russian request could be refused, since no change would be in train.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1062:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Caffery in Paris on July 20, 1945. He has written to Molotov that day, proposing Soviet participation in supervising the Greek elections. The letter follows the text Washington proposed on July 17.

Byrnes asks Caffery to make a like proposal to the French government at once. He adds one caution, suggested by the British delegation and accepted by him. No publicity should be given the proposal. Silence must hold until the French and Soviet replies arrive, and the Greek government can be properly informed. The exchange belongs to the Potsdam Conference record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1162:
A working group with a long name, the Subcommittee on Cooperation in Solving Immediate European Economic Problems, reported on 25 July 1945. Its charge was the crisis on the ground. While leaders debated grand plans, this group faced hunger, cold, and idle factories across a ruined continent.

The report urged the three powers to work jointly on relief and recovery. Food, coal, and transport could not wait for perfect politics. Findings of this kind fed the summit's choices on aid and trade. The paper is Potsdam at its most practical: policy aimed at empty stomachs and dark homes, written by staff who saw the need up close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1262:
General Somervell, who commanded the Army Service Forces, wrote to Leathers, Britain's Minister of War Transport, on 20 July 1945. Somervell's command fed, clothed, and moved the American army around the world. Leathers ran the British side of wartime transport.

A letter between the two supply chiefs joined the logistics of both nations at the top. Ports, ships, rail, and stores all had to serve one plan as the war shifted east. This message shows that joint supply world at work during the summit. The peace talks sat on a mountain of moved goods, and men like these moved it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1362:
The British Embassy in Washington delivered a note to the Department of State on 28 July 1945. Embassy notes are formal papers, worded with care and meant for the record. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A note from an embassy speaks for its government in full, unlike a chat or a cable between friends. Britain and the United States were close allies in 1945, but allies still put hard points in writing. This note reached the department while its leaders were at Potsdam, so it landed on the desks of the men holding the fort. It shows allied business being done in the capital even with the summit under way abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-162:
Benjamin Cohen took these notes on August 1, 1945, the final day of the Potsdam Conference. His notes stand in the second Potsdam volume beside the formal minutes. Cohen watched the legal shape of the closing acts. The day's work fixed texts that governments would cite for years.

Final-day notes by a lawyer have lasting use. Later arguments about Potsdam turned on commas and clauses. Cohen's record helps readers judge what was meant at the time. The notes also close his personal run of witness. Few staff papers in the volume combine nearness and care as his do.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-62:
A United States delegation memo sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 22, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Four heads of business are reported from the Sunday morning session.

On the Yalta declaration, the ministers agreed to report no agreement on election observation. That was paragraph 1 of the U.S. paper on liberated areas. The press and control commission paragraphs went to a subcommittee instead. It would study recent improvements in the commissions in Bulgaria, Rumania, and Hungary. It would also study Soviet complaints about the Allied body in Italy. On German economics, several paragraphs of the draft principles were approved, with more discussion to come. On Rumanian oil equipment, extended discussion produced no agreement at all on how British and U.S. gear there should be treated.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d762:
The Acting Secretary wrote to John Erhardt, political adviser for Austrian affairs, on July 21, 1945. Document 762 carries Washington's guidance to the man handling Austria. Austria, freed from German rule, awaited its own settlement. Erhardt worked where Allied occupation was taking shape. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Guidance letters like this one turned summit talk into field action. Erhardt needed to know how far he could go. Readers see the chain from a Washington desk to an adviser among the occupying powers. The document shows Austria's quieter file moving beside the conference's louder ones. Small posts felt Potsdam's reach too.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d862:
Dated July 20, 1945, at Babelsberg, this United States delegation working paper offers draft wording for the Potsdam talks on Germany. It was prepared for the Economic Sub-Committee that morning. The paper gives one numbered clause, paragraph 17, on how the occupation should handle reparations and imports.

The clause says a main aim of occupation is reparation for harm done by German aggression. It calls on the Control Council to set a program of minimum imports for Germany as a whole. Supplies inside Germany should be shared fairly among the zones. Paying back money advanced for approved imports would come first from the proceeds of German exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d962: American delegates added this short clause to their reparations proposal on July 30, 1945. It answers a practical question: who decides how much factory equipment is surplus to a peace economy, and thus open to reparations? The answer given is the Reparation Commission, with France added to its membership. The commission would consult the Control Council as it worked. Even then, the zone commander of the zone losing the equipment keeps the final say. A file note credits the draft of this addition to Secretary Byrnes himself.
frus-1947v05-d62: Another 1947 FRUS document from the Near East and Africa volume. The Acting Secretary addressed regional affairs. This entry preserves that record. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
frus-1969-76v38p1-d62: A 1969-1976 FRUS document from the foundations of foreign policy volume, 1973-1976. The later Nixon and Ford years. This entry preserves that record. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gadbury-collectio-geniturarum-1662:
John Gadbury was a Restoration astrologer who feuded in print with rivals for decades. His Collectio Geniturarum, published in 1662, gathers a collection of one hundred and fifty nativities, birth charts of real people. The book is the great Restoration case-book of judicial astrology.

Each chart comes with the events of the life it maps: offices, marriages, illnesses, and deaths read against the planets. Gadbury meant the cases to prove the art by its hits, as a lawyer proves a rule by precedents. Students of the period still mine his collection for the lives it records in passing.
gao-gaoreports-b-295462: Lucent Technologies World Services brought its March 2005 dispute to GAO, and the ruling delivers the call. The telecom heavyweight's protest got the standard full review. Size buys no shortcuts at the referee's desk. The desk stayed neutral. The call was neutral.
gao-gaoreports-b-295562: Singleton Enterprises carried its February 2005 dispute to GAO, and the ruling renders the judgment. The firm's claims faced the referee squarely. The protest got its full hearing and more. The hearing was complete. The judgment was rendered. The dispute was settled.
gao-gaoreports-b-297262: Metro Home Medical Supply took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Medical suppliers get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298662: Advanced Federal Services took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298962: Palmetto GBA doubled its January 2007 protest — two case numbers, one health-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299862: Charleston Marine Containers fought a 2007 award at GAO — and this ruling is the decision. The box-maker said the agency's pick was wrong; the call tests the claim and rules. In the unglamorous world of shipping-container contracts, fair-bidding law applies just the same.
gao-gaoreports-b-302962: NARA's records center fund got a fiscal ruling in this 2005 GAO call, which tests property damage recovery. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the recovery was legal. The law had the final word. The recovery had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-308762: Homeland Security's internal money shuffling got a legal once-over from GAO in 2007 — were the shared-service deals inside its Preparedness wing kosher? The ruling reads the purse statutes against the department's bookkeeping. Even a young giant, GAO reminds, must color inside the budget lines.
gao-gaoreports-b-310762: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by PM Services Company. The February 4, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-262: The SEC's cyber locks were weak in 2005, and GAO's report says the commission had to address poor controls over financial and sensitive data. The review sounds the alarm. The market's secrets deserved the guard. The controls had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-462: Perchlorate tracking needed a system in 2005, and GAO's report says a way to track sampling and cleanup results was required. The findings demand the tool. The report warns that the tainted water deserved monitoring. The system had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-762: The federal student loan repayment program needed better administration in 2005, and GAO's report says OPM could build on efforts to help agencies. The findings demand the support. The report warns that the indebted workers deserved help. The efforts had to be built upon.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-162: China trade was rising but the U.S. share was falling in 2006, and GAO's report says exports and investment grew while the share declined. The findings do the math. The report warns that the dragon's market needed honest measuring. The trends had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-362: Hurt troops' disability calls needed better eyes in 2006, and GAO's report says the system wanted firmer watching for fair, fast results. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the wounded deserved fair and quick calls. The watching had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-62: Medicare's equipment payment formula got a GAO verdict in 2006, and the report says Class III devices did not warrant a distinct annual update. The findings do the math. The report warns that the device dollars deserved fair formulas. The update was not warranted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-762: America's Middle East broadcasts needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says the broadcasting services could be improved. The findings tune the dials. The report warns that the airwaves' message needed sharper delivery. The management had to improve. The signal had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-962: Force planning needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to integrate data into its force identification process. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the troop requirements should not be guesswork. The data had to drive the decisions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1062: Inflation had quietly shrunk the sting of tax penalties by 2007 — GAO's report does the deflating math. Fines fixed in old dollars punished less with each passing year. The findings make a dry but pointed case: penalties that do not keep up with prices stop deterring.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1162: Sticky notes on the fridge were not cutting it — GAO's 2007 report says Washington could teach homes far more about saving energy. From bulb labels to public drives, the report grades the government's consumer coaching. Smarter tips, GAO argues, would trim family bills and national demand in one stroke.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-462: The Senate's restaurants got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the revolving fund's finances for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion for the record in full detail. The report proves the watchdog's reach extends from missiles to meatloaf.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-62: The government's big surveys needed a rethink in 2007, and GAO's report says the portfolio of major household surveys deserved reexamination. The findings demand the review. The report warns that the nation's questionnaires should not waste the nation's time. The surveys had to earn their keep.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-762: Hanford's glass-log gamble needed a second look in 2007 — GAO's report says the Energy Department should rethink the bulk vitrification demo for the tank waste. The findings question the tech bet. The report's caution: billion-dollar demos deserve proof before they get permits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1062: GAO published its findings on pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: Need for Improved Oversight Persists in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-162: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at embassy Security: Upgrades Have Enhanced Security, but Site Conditions Prevent Full Adherence to Standards. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-262: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at natural Resource Management: Opportunities Exist to Enhance Federal Participation in Collaborative Efforts to Reduce Conflicts and Improve Natural Resource Cond. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-862: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at international Marriage Broker Regulation Act of 2005: Agencies Have Implemented Some, but Not All of the Act's Requirements. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Between 1954 and 1962 the United States built a nuclear presence across Western Europe, stationing American weapons with allied forces under shared-control arrangements. This briefing-book page is the first part of an Archive set on that deployment. The evidence here is the title alone, and the documents in this part are not described. Those years set the pattern that still governs American weapons in Europe: bombs stored on allied soil, owned by Washington, and surrounded by political arrangements every host government must defend.
heydon-holy-guide-1662:
John Heydon published The Holy Guide in London in 1662, subtitled as leading the way to the wonder of the world. The massive volume is a Rosicrucian compendium. Astrology, geomancy, and Rosie-Crucian physic fill its books, making it the most encyclopedic English Rosicrucian work of the seventeenth century.

Heydon compiles, adapts, and expands earlier writers with a free hand. Star lore and earth divination stand beside recipes for the Rosicrucian medicine. His ambition is total: one book for the whole art. Critics of his day charged him with borrowing without shame. Modern readers value the Guide as a warehouse of the period's occult knowledge, gathered by its most industrious English salesman.
homestead-act-1862:
Congress passed the Homestead Act in 1862, and Lincoln signed it into law. Any settler who farmed public land for five years could own it. One hundred sixty acres came free to those who proved the claim.

Millions of claims followed as families poured onto the plains. The family farm became national policy in the act's plain terms. Towns, schools, and whole states rose from its quarter-section grants. Native peoples paid the price as their lands passed to settlers. The law that settled a continent still shapes the West's map and memory. Its grid of farms can still be seen from any plane window.
huxley-on-fossil-remains-of-man-1862:
Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's most forceful defender, lectured on fossil human remains in 1862. He spoke at the Royal Institution with very little material to work from. The Engis and Neanderthal skulls formed nearly the whole evidence.

Huxley compares those skulls with modern human and ape skulls, bone by bone. He finds no barrier that separates fossil humans from living ones. The lecture builds a Darwinian reading of human antiquity from scant bones. Its confidence helped set the tone for his famous book on man's place in nature the next year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowy-jacob-ezek:
Jacob Ezekiel Löwy (1814–1864) was a German rabbi and author born at Hotzenplotz in Austrian Silesia, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch. After study at several yeshivahs and a turn toward Hasidism at Lemberg and Brody, he gained secular learning at Berlin. He worked in business before taking rabbinic posts.

In 1846 Löwy became district rabbi of Wadowice, seated at Oswiecin, and in 1854 he was elected rabbi of Beuthen, where he stayed until his death. The article names his one book, a critical Talmudic lexicon printed at Vienna in 1863. It held 150 articles meant as the start of a full Talmudic encyclopedia, but only the first volume appeared. The entry preserves both a rabbi’s winding path to office and an ambitious reference project left unfinished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maghariyyah-al-:
Al-Maghariyyah, an early Jewish sect, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The Arabic name means Men of the Caves. Kirkisani reports that the sect began in the first century before the common era. It took its name from keeping its books hidden in caves.

The article sets out the sect's beliefs. Its members counted months from the new moon and banned games of every kind. They rejected all pictures of God as a manlike being. God was too high, they held, to deal directly with matter. So an angel created the world as God's agent, and the Law itself came through that angel. Harkavy identified the group with the Essenes, who also lived apart in desert places. He even read its Alexandrian author as Philo, whose Logos matches the angel idea. The entry preserves a sect known only through the reports of others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manetti-giannoz:
Giannozzo Manetti, an Italian statesman and Christian Hebraist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Florence in 1396, he became a secretary to Pope Nicholas V. At the pope's suggestion he learned Hebrew from a Jew named Manuel. He died at Naples on October 26, 1459.

The article lists the fruits of that study. He kept a Jewish servant with whom he spoke Hebrew. His son Agnolo learned Hebrew beside Latin and Greek from an early age. At the pope's request Manetti translated the Psalms into Latin. He had to defend his translation method in a special treatise. Hoping for the pope's prize of 5,000 ducats, he hunted for a Hebrew original of Matthew's Gospel. The Hebrew manuscripts he gathered are now in the Vatican. He also began a large work of argument against the Jews. The entry shows Renaissance Hebrew learning at its most ambitious.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maskileison-abr:
Abraham Maskileison was a Russian rabbi and Talmud scholar. Herman Rosenthal and N. T. London profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1788 and served as rabbi in many cities. In his later years he settled at Minsk, and he died there in 1848. He was descended from R. Israel Jaffe of Shklov, an author of note.

The entry stresses character as much as scholarship: Maskileison knew the Cabala but refused to earn money from it, as miracle-working rabbis did. He lived in near poverty on a small income and gave his whole life to study. His books are Talmudic novellae, fresh readings of the text. “Maskil le-Etan” came out at Shklov in 1818. “Be'er Abraham” came out at Wilna in the year of his death, and several more volumes came out after he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-meir-ba-al:
Meir, the second-century tanna remembered as Ba'al ha-Nes, the miracle-worker, is introduced in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé. Born in Asia Minor, he is wrapped in mystery from the start: legend made him a descendant of the emperor Nero, said to have escaped death and converted. Even "Meir," meaning "one who enlightens," was a title earned by teaching, not his birth name.

The entry follows his schooling from Akiba, whose lectures at first outran him, to Ishmael, and back to Akiba, who ordained him above older disciples. Meir kept clear of Bar Kokba's revolt but suffered in its fallout: his father-in-law died a martyr, and his sister-in-law was carried to a Roman brothel. The famous rescue tale that follows, built on the cry "Meir's God, help me," explains the miracle-worker's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelsohn-samu:
Samuel Mendelsohn was an American rabbi and scholar. Cyrus Adler profiles him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Shillelen in the province of Kovno in 1850. He trained at the rabbinical college of Wilna, the rabbinic school of Berlin, and Maimonides College in Philadelphia. He spent three years as rabbi of Congregation Beth-El in Norfolk, Virginia. In 1876 he moved to the Temple of Israel at Wilmington, North Carolina. He was still serving there when the entry was written. The University of North Carolina gave him an honorary doctorate of laws in 1883.

His scholarly monument is "The Criminal Jurisprudence of the Ancient Hebrews," published at Baltimore in 1891. Pamphlets and many articles in the Jewish press of two continents stand beside it. The entry closes with his marriage into the Jastrow family. It notes his son Charles's fellowship in classics at the University of Pennsylvania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-samuel-10:
Samuel Meyer, born in Hanover on February 26, 1819, was a German rabbi whose career is summarized in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling. He studied Talmud in Hanover and Frankfurt and attended the University of Bonn. In 1845 he succeeded Nathan Adler as district rabbi of Hanover and Lüneburg.

Two years later Meyer carried out Adler's plan to found a teachers' seminary in Hanover, a lasting mark on Jewish education there. His own writings were modest: a few sermons, an 1862 history of the synagogue community's charitable society, and an edition of poems by Abraham ibn Ezra that he had discovered in manuscript. He died in Hanover in 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minsk-formerly-:
Minsk was the capital of the Russian government of the same name. Its Jewish history is kept in royal decrees. Herman Rosenthal, Max Rosenthal, and Peter Wiernik assemble them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Very little is otherwise known, the article admits. In 1576 Stephen Bathori licensed its Jews to engage in any trade. By the century's end they were expelled from Lithuania with the rest.

In 1606 Jews were back, owning shops. Yet the king at the same time confirmed their expulsion. He annulled it in 1616 and restored the old privileges. In 1625 the community gained permanent possession of its synagogue and cemetery grounds. In 1629 it might own stores but not build houses. Ladislaus IV let them buy lots and build shops. Houses, though, still came only through debt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montezinos-anto:
Antonio de Montezinos, also called Aaron Levi, was a Marrano traveler. His report of lost Israelites in America changed English policy. Gotthard Deutsch and Joseph Jacobs tell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Journeying near Quito about 1641, he met natives, he claimed, who practiced Jewish ceremonies. They recited the Shema. They were men of the tribe of Reuben, with Levites beyond them.

In 1644 he carried the tale to Amsterdam. He told it to Manasseh ben Israel. Manasseh printed it in his Hope of Israel. He passed it to Thomas Thorowgood's Jews in America. The entry gives the claim straight. Its bibliography points to Lucien Wolf's study of Manasseh's mission to Cromwell. That was the mission the story helped launch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-arles-:
Moses of Arles was a French scholar of the second half of the tenth century. Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is the earliest scholar of the city of Arles of whom there is definite knowledge. Only one piece of his writing has been preserved.

It is an answer on a point of religious law, in a civil case laid before Kalonymus, probably the poet Kalonymus of Lucca. The answer survives because later works, such as the Mordekai, quoted it. His son, Judah ben Moses of Arles, also became a rabbinical authority. The brief entry marks the first named point on the map of Jewish learning in Provence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-worms-:
Moses of Worms is a legendary rabbi of the eleventh century, famed in story as the greatest magician of his time. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, draws on the chronicle of Tritheim. In the legend, Archbishop Eberhard of Treves moved against the Jews in 1066.

Eberhard ordered that Jews who refused baptism on the Saturday before Easter must leave the country. As he prepared for a general baptism of the Jews, he died suddenly. The tale says the Jews of Treves had appealed to Moses of Worms for help. Moses made a wax figure of the archbishop and burned it while reciting spells. The entry keeps the story labeled as legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-judah-be:
Nathan Judah ben Solomon was a Provençal doctor and translator. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the fourteenth century, probably at Avignon. His Provençal names were En Bongodas and Bonjues. His family added a phrase claiming descent from David's house.

Nathan turned science from Arabic into Hebrew. His versions covered drugs, fevers, and the care of the head. He rendered Ghazali on philosophy and Arnaud on wines. Those translations still survive only in manuscript copies. He began one of them young, at his master's request. He also wrote a letter defending the study of philosophy. Orthodox critics had attacked that study, and he answered them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebuchadnezzar-:
Nebuchadnezzar was Babylon's king and Jerusalem's destroyer. Emil G. Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, Wilhelm Bacher, and Louis Ginzberg wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Nabopolassar, founder of the empire. His name means, roughly, Nebo defend my boundary. It appears over ninety times in the Old Testament.

He broke Egypt's army at the Euphrates early on. Judah's kings served him, rebelled, and served again. In 598 he took King Jehoiakim and thousands of captives. He set Zedekiah on the throne in 597. When Zedekiah rebelled with Egypt's help, siege followed. Jerusalem fell in 586 after eighteen hard months. Zedekiah's sons were slain, his eyes put out. The Temple burned and its vessels went to Babylon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-b-reuben:
Nissim b. Reuben Gerondi, the RaN, taught at Barcelona. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He flourished there from about 1340 to 1380. He was a physician, an astronomer, and a halakist. Wealthy Jews slandered him before the government then.

Nissim thought clearly and dared to differ from giants. He refuted Rashi, Maimonides, and Naḥmanides where he disagreed. Yet in practice he kept the ancients' rulings with care. His Alfasi commentaries aim at decisions for daily life. He wrote the first full commentary on Nedarim. Some thousand responsa of his once circulated widely. Only seventy-seven of them have been preserved. His pupil Isaac b. Sheshet called him his age's foremost rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orhot-zaddikim-:
Orhot Zaddikim is a book on right conduct and good traits. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was written in Germany in the fourteen hundreds. Its author called it Sefer ha-Middot, the Book of Traits. A later scribe gave it the name it now bears.

No one knows who wrote the book for sure. One guess names Lipmann Mühlhausen as its author. It was meant as a code of traits for all folk. A German Jewish version came out at Isny in 1542. The Hebrew text came out at Prague in 1581. It was then printed oft in both tongues for years. Its rules warn that pride is an evil trait in man. They urge a man to be just, meek, and kind to all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pale-of-settlem:
The Pale of Settlement was a part of Russia set for Jews. Herman Rosenthal wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews were let live in that part, and not past it. Other Russians could live where they chose in the realm. Jews held no such right as a rule of law.

Jews could leave the Pale just on set terms in law. The Pale was first set up in the year 1791. White Russian Jews had passed to Russian rule in 1772. That change came with the first split of Poland then. They were barred from guilds in other parts of Russia. Queen Catherine gave them rights in two new lands then. Those lands were Yekaterinoslav and the Taurida tract. The bounds of the Pale have shifted since that time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pineles-hirsch-:
Hirsch Mendel Pineles was a Galician scholar of the Talmud. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tysmenitz in 1805 and died in 1870. At fifteen he moved to Brody and married. He ended his days at Galatz, in Rumania.

At Brody Pineles took up German and astronomy. The Hasidim there charged him with heresy for it. He cleared himself before his father-in-law. His great work, Darkah shel Torah, came out in 1861. It defends the Mishnah against its own later explainers. Angry replies followed from his contemporaries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pomegranate-pun:
The pomegranate is a tree of the myrtle family, known in Latin as Punica granatum. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tree reached Egypt in very early times. It grew in Palestine, Assyria, and most lands by the Mediterranean Sea.

Spies brought pomegranates back as proof that Canaan was rich land. The fruit stood among the common trees of the country. A famed tree grew at Gibeah in the days of Saul. The Song of Solomon praises its flower and fruit again and again. Carved pomegranates adorned the two great Temple pillars. The fruit was stitched on the robe of the high priest. In the East it stands for full life and plenty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quietus-lusius-:
Lusius Quietus was a Roman general who ruled Judea in 117. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a Moorish prince by birth. His skill in war won him the favor of Trajan. The emperor marked him out as his heir, it is said.

On Trajan's march in Parthia, the Jews of Babylonia rose. Quietus put that rising down with no mercy shown. The governorship of Judea was his reward for the work. Church writers of old tell the tale of his rule. The article builds his life from those scant sources. It places him in the last Jewish wars under Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-randegger-maier:
Maier Randegger was an Austrian teacher born on February 9, 1780. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Randegg and taught first in Vienna. He died at Triest on March 12, 1853.

The article traces his schooling in Switzerland, Bavaria, and Presburg. At Triest he opened a private school and settled for life. He taught at Fiume and Fiorenzuola from 1838 to 1847. Twice he filled in as rabbi at Triest. His works include Zinnat Dawid and a Haggadah. The Haggadah had an Italian version by his daughter. The entry honors a teacher who served schools and synagogues alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reifmann-jacob-:
Jacob Reifmann was a Russian author and philosopher born on April 7, 1818. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Lagow near Opatow. He died at Szczebrzeszyn on October 13, 1895.

The article describes his scattered early Talmud study. Teachers chose random passages, and no volume was finished. At fifteen he began to study on his own. Logic became the guide for his study and writing. He married into a home rich in books at Szczebrzeszyn. There he found Maimonides and Judah ha-Levi waiting. He read them with zeal until he knew them by heart. German philosophy then opened a new world to him. The entry traces a self made thinker.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rimini-12762:
Rimini is an Italian town on the Adriatic coast. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lies about twenty eight miles from Forli. Its fame here rests on Hebrew printing.

The article says Gershon Soncino produced many works there. His Rimini period ran from 1521 to 1526. He printed the third edition of the Siddur Romagna in 1521. That edition is the rarest of them, they note. Joseph Albo's Ikkarim followed in 1522. Bahya on the Pentateuch came across 1524 to 1526. Rashi's commentary also appeared in 1526. Steinschneider's catalogue is the entry's single source. The short record marks a brief golden age of print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-david:
David Augustus Rosenthal was a German physician and author born at Neisse, Silesia, in 1812. Isidore Singer and Bernhard Pick wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Breslau and died there in 1875.

In 1851 Rosenthal embraced Roman Catholicism and worked to lift its press in Silesia. His literary career opened with an edition of the poet Angelus Silesius. From 1869 to 1872 he issued his Convertitenbilder in four volumes. It sketches Jews and Protestants who became Catholics in the nineteenth century. The entry calls it a major source for that century's church history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbath-12962:
The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week, the Jewish day of rest. Its four authors were Emil G. Hirsch, Joseph Jacobs, the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, and Julius H. Greenstone. The entry opens with the Bible's own data on the day.

Genesis says God blessed and hallowed the seventh day after creation. The Ten Commandments order Israel to remember it and keep it holy. During the manna story, a double portion fell the day before each Sabbath. Breaking the day by work could bring death under the law. Deuteronomy adds rest for servants, recalling the Exodus from Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sambation-sanba:
The Sambation is the river beyond which the ten lost tribes were exiled. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rabbinic literature names it, and legends later grew around it.

The Targum to Exodus says Israel would be placed beyond the River Sambation. Genesis Rabbah adds that Judah and Benjamin went elsewhere in exile. No early passage tells where the river's name came from, the entry stresses. It seems to have been a river of Media in Persia. Nahmanides identified it with the biblical Gozan of Assyrian exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schey-philipp-b:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Philipp Schey, Baron von Koromla. He was a Hungarian merchant and giver to charity. Schey was born at Güns on September 20, 1798. He died at Baden, near Vienna, on June 28, 1881. He was the first Jew in Hungary raised to Austrian nobility.

Emperor Francis Joseph granted Schey's patent on May 13, 1859. The patent praises his service to the dynasty in the revolution of 1848 and 1849. It also honors his great kindness toward suffering people. That kindness, it says, ignored all differences of creed. The entry is short and rests on Reich's Beth-El. It marks a milestone for Hungarian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sea-mew-13362: Joseph Jacobs and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the sea-mew. For the Bible's data it points readers to the article Cuckoo. The Talmud names an unclean bird in the tractate Ḥullin. Rashi explains that name as a very lean bird. Some scholars link the Talmudic words to the Latin prava, meaning bad. Others link them to a Greek word for meager or dry. On that reading, the birds are species of the sea-mew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sforno-13462:
Sforno was an Italian family that produced many rabbis and scholars. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the family. Hananeel ben Jacob Sforno taught Talmud at Bologna around 1500. His brother Obadiah became the family's most famous name.

Israel Sforno gave legal rulings quoted in a large Italian collection. Jacob ben Obadiah Sforno, a Venetian scholar, was credited with a mystic work. Scholars later doubted that the book was truly his. The entry works like a family tree of learning. Readers meet several generations who kept Italian Jewish scholarship alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silesia-11662:
Silesia is a Prussian province, once Austrian, with a Jewish history reaching back centuries. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the region. Unreliable tales date its first Jewish settlement to the eleventh century. A firm community likely formed in the twelfth century instead.

Early settlements clustered at Breslau, Bunzlau, Glogau, and other towns. Many first settlers were poor and spoke Slavonic tongues. One man often served as rabbi, teacher, and prayer leader. Some had fled the Crusaders' violence in the west. Others immigrated from Bohemia and Poland nearby. Doubtful reports tell of early persecution and wall building. The entry sorts legend from record with open care. It gives readers a careful start on Silesian Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siloam-inscript:
Siloam Inscription is the carved text found on Jerusalem's ancient Siloam water conduit. Emil G. Hirsch and Philippe Berger wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. It is the earliest long Hebrew inscription found at Jerusalem. Indeed, it may be the only truly important one in Palestine.

The inscription marks the digging of the city's famed waterway. That digging was a great event in Jerusalem's story. The Bible mentions the waterway more than once, the entry notes. Two deep valleys nearly surround the ancient city. The Tyropoeon valley runs between them through its center. Ophel, the spur by the Temple hill, frames the site. The entry explains the ground before reading the stones. Readers see why one tunnel text matters so much.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sin-13762: Sin names two places in this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Emil G Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote it, and it appeared in 1906. The first Sin is an Egyptian city named in Ezekiel. It was likely Pelusium, the old frontier fortress. The second is a desert on the Sinai Peninsula, between Elim and Sinai. Israel camped there during the Exodus wanderings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stork-hasidah-1:
The stork is a bird the Bible lists as unclean for food. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Hebrew name is ḥasidah. That name hints at the piety the ancients credited to storks. Leviticus and Deuteronomy both name it among banned birds.

Both white and black storks occur in Palestine. The white stork passes through in April on migration. The black stork gathers near the Dead Sea. Talmudic sources treat ḥasidah as a term of praise. They say the bird shares its food with its fellows. One tradition claims its gall cures a scorpion bite. The entry blends Bible, nature, and rabbinic lore on one bird.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synagogue-the-g:
The Great Synagogue was the assembly that carried the Law after the Prophets. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. The Mishnah places its men in the chain of tradition. Prophets transmitted the Torah to them in that chain. Simon the Just survived from their number.

Later versions name Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi as links. Those three prophets likely sat among the members themselves. Rabbi Johanan credited the assembly with fixing Israel's prayers. Their benedictions still shape Jewish worship today. The body bridged prophecy and the named rabbis. Antigonus of Soko received the Torah after them. The entry sorts conflicting accounts of one founding body. It shows how tradition remembered its own handover.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tatnai-r-v-tatt:
Tatnai was a governor under King Darius of Persia. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Ezra names him governor of Coele-Syria. The Revised Version spells his name Tattenai. He tried to halt the Temple's rebuilding at Jerusalem.

Tatnai questioned Zerubbabel and Jeshua as they built. He wrote to Darius asking for an archive search. The Jews claimed Cyrus had licensed the work. Tatnai wanted proof from the royal records. Scholars read his Persian name as Thithinaya or Thathanaia. The Septuagint and Josephus transcribe it differently again. The brief entry preserves the official who tested Judah's claim. His letter set the stage for Darius's reply.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theology-14362:
Jewish theology, the ordered teaching about God and the world, is defined here. Kaufmann Kohler and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It speaks from the standpoint of Orthodox Judaism. On that view, God revealed true doctrine through chosen prophets.

Moses stands first among those prophets. When prophecy ended, revelation ended with it. Scripture and oral tradition carry the revealed truths still. No human doctrine may add to or annul them. Yet natural theology also earns a place. Reason, itself a gift from God, cannot clash with revelation. Jewish thinkers thus test revealed truth with the mind. Faith and reason work side by side here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toulon-hebr-144:
Toulon, a Provençal port city, held a Jewish community in medieval times. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Under the counts of Provence its Jews met mixed treatment. Kindness and oppression alternated over the years. The Black Death brought the worst blow in 1348.

Neighbors accused Toulon's Jews of poisoning wells and springs. Forty Jews were killed in a single night. The entry names two scholars of the city. Berechiah ben Azariah owned a fourteenth-century Talmud codex. Astrue of Toulon helped publish an early Hebrew book. By 1905 about thirty Jewish families remained. They belonged to the Marseilles consistory district.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ujhely-satoralj:
Ujhely, a city in Hungary's Zemplin county, had Jews owning land by 1734. Gotthard Deutsch and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its archives show the community growing steadily then. Its school received a huge bequest in 1829. The school took donor Martin Kästenbaum's name afterward.

The oldest tombstone there dates to 1760. A burial society with a hospital formed in 1772. A synagogue rose in 1790 on the site. Its demolition in 1887 revealed eight underground chambers. Rabbi Moses Teitelbaum led the community until 1841. Legend says he blessed the infant Louis Kossuth there. Orthodox leader Jeremiah Löw succeeded in that pulpit. About 4,500 Jews lived among 13,000 residents in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waldstein-charl:
Charles Waldstein was an Anglo American archaeologist. He was born in New York on March 30, 1856. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Columbia, Heidelberg, and Cambridge. In 1880 he began lecturing on classical archaeology at Cambridge. He directed the Fitzwilliam Museum from 1883.

In 1889 Waldstein went to Athens. He directed the American School of Classical Studies there. His teams dug at Plataea and at Eretria. At Argos they uncovered the great Heraeum. He claimed to have found Aristotle's tomb as well. In 1895 he returned to Cambridge as Slade professor. His books cover Greek art and the Jewish question.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-werber-baruch-1:
Baruch Werber was an Austrian Hebraist and editor. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Brody, in Galicia, early in the eighteen hundreds. He died there on July 31, 1876. He followed the scholars Isaac Erter and Nachman Krochmal.

Werber founded a Hebrew weekly at Brody. It ran from 1865 to 1890 under two titles. He wrote notes on Ecclesiastes with a long preface. That work appeared at Lemberg in 1862. He also wrote a life of Albert Cohn of Paris. His son Jacob later took over the paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-the-youn:
Yannai the Younger was a scholar of Palestine of the fourth rank. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Men called him the Younger to split him from Yannai ben Ishmael. His name zeera marks his youth in the Hebrew tongue.

When his father-in-law died, a rite rule was waived for him. He was let to tend the dead in that hard case. One of his lines on oaths lives on in a midrash. It treats how an oath is sworn and why it binds. At his own burial his pupils broke with custom. Rabbi Mani rebuked them for that break in print. The short entry rests on three learned books of the past. It gives few facts, but it keeps his name and rank clear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zangwill-israel:
Israel Zangwill (born 1864) was an English man of letters from London. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. As a boy he moved with his kin to Bristol. He went to school there and then back in London. He taught at the Jews' Free School in that city.

He took a degree at London at the same time. A clash with the heads of the school made him quit. He then gave his whole life to books and print. As a boy he had made a Purim sheet in 1880. In 1888 his first long tale came out in print. He wrote that tale with a co-worker named Cowen. Its style owes a debt to two great English pens. He then ran a wit sheet with a set of young wits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zimri-15262:
Zimri is a name borne by several men in the Bible, and one by a short-lived king. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One Zimri was a grandson of Judah. Another, a Simeonite prince, was killed by Phinehas after bringing a Midianite woman into the camp at Shittim.

The best-known Zimri was a chariot captain who murdered King Elah and seized the throne of Israel. He held it only seven days. When the army chose Omri instead, Zimri burned the palace at Tirzah over himself and died in the flames. The entry also notes a Benjamite Zimri and the kings of Zimri named by Jeremiah.
lady-mary-wortley-montague-her-life-and-:
Lewis Melville wrote this life of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, covering 1689 to 1762. Seventeen pictures illustrate the book. Its first chapter treats her childhood and the Pierrepont family.

Lady Mary learned Latin as a girl and loved reading early. Her father later became Earl of Kingston. The book follows her through marriage, travel, and famous letters. Melville draws on her own writing across the chapters. Readers meet one of England's sharpest letter writers through both her story and her words. Her Turkish letters later made her name across Europe. This life places those letters within a full, eventful career.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume three of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter eighteen. The King of Spain lies in weak health, with no heir. Each court in Europe takes up the question of his vast lands.

William III of England puts forth a plan to split the succession. Spain and the Indies would go to the Archduke, by that plan. France would gain Naples, Sicily, and Lorraine in the split. The Emperor refuses to hear of a split, and the secret plan leaks out. Spain's ambassador spoke so boldly that William sent him out. Court pride abroad matches court pride at home in these pages.
mommsen-history-rome-vol-1-1862:
Theodor Mommsen's History of Rome appears here in William P. Dickson's translation of 1862. Volume 1 covers Rome from its legendary founding to the eve of the Punic Wars. Mommsen rebuilds the early Republic: its laws, tribes, wars, and constitution. His learning drew on inscriptions and coins as well as texts.

Mommsen writes with the confidence of a liberal who knew modern politics too. His Rome feels alive, partisan, and legally precise. The work later won him the Nobel Prize in Literature. No reconstruction of the Republic has replaced his in scope. Volume 1 is the gateway to a monumental history. Dickson's version served English readers for generations.
nasa-tm-19650009357-sweden-operations-19:
C D Tackett reported for Goddard's Sounding Rocket Instrumentation Section on rocket work done in Sweden in 1962. Small Nike-Cajun sounding rockets were fired there to study noctilucent clouds. Those are faint, high clouds that glow at night. Working in another country added its own problems.

Tackett focuses chiefly on telemetry instrumentation, its problems, successes, and failures. He also records personal and technical experience from the campaign. The stated aim was to keep the information for future reference and study. Readers get a field record, not just a results table.
openalex-w2033075062:
Sarah Tubiana, Marc Mikulski, Jerome Becam and colleagues looked for warning signs of severe leptospirosis. Their study appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. Leptospirosis is a major health concern in New Caledonia. A small share of infections become severe. Doctors knew little about who is at risk.

The team compared hospital patients with severe and milder disease. Records came from two public hospitals over several years. Smoking was linked with severe disease. Waiting over two days to start antibiotics also raised risk. One bacterial strain group was tied to severe cases too. Some blood test results after admission predicted poor outcomes. Early treatment and close monitoring may save lives.
openalex-w2120599762:
Fabien Anthelme, Lohengrin Cavieres, and Olivier Dangles published this review in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. They asked how help between plants, not just competition, shapes alpine plant groups as the climate warms. High mountain plants often grow better near a sheltering neighbor than alone in harsh wind and cold.

The authors review recent studies and argue that positive help is still left out of most models that predict climate effects. They explain the stress-gradient idea, which says help grows stronger as conditions get harsher. Their point is that warming will change these plant partnerships, so forecasts that count only competition will miss much of what happens.
openalex-w2169861662:
Christian Ganoza, Michael Matthias, Devon Collins-Richards, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2006. Severe leptospirosis, a bacterial disease from animal urine in water, struck city districts of Iquitos, Peru, but not nearby rural areas. The team tested whether dangerous bacteria concentrate more in urban surface waters.

A sensitive gene test measured Leptospira in waters from both settings. Disease-causing species turned up only in urban slum water sources, at far higher levels than in rural water. One strain in market gutter water matched bacteria from human patients exactly, pointing to spread from rats to people. In a fever study, catching that strain was tied to urban exposure.
openalex-w2346770762:
Luis Chavez, Mónica León, Sharon Einav, and Joseph Varon published this systematic review in Critical Care in 2016. Rhabdomyolysis, the breakdown of skeletal muscle spilling its contents into the blood, can wreck the kidneys. The literature on it is a tangle of rival definitions and treatments, so the authors set out to summarize what is actually known.

They screened over five thousand papers from a decade across three databases, keeping fifty-six. Most studies define the syndrome by a key muscle enzyme five times above the normal limit. Causes differ between adults and children. Strikingly, no randomized trials have ever tested plain IV fluids against fluids plus bicarbonate or mannitol, the standard add-ons. The review lays out the gaps plainly for clinicians.
openalex-w2463100762:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this letter in Physical Review Letters in 2010. Among the first results from the new Large Hadron Collider, it measures how charged particles spray from proton collisions at seven TeV. Knowing this basic spray pattern is the foundation for spotting anything rare in the debris.

The team charted particles' sideways momentum and their spread along the beam direction. Most particles come from soft interactions that theory can only model roughly. These measurements give the model builders hard targets to tune against. They also set the proton baseline for judging how lead-ion collisions change particle production. The paper is a reference point the whole collider program still builds on.
openalex-w2555900862:
Blanca Román-Viñas, Jean-Philippe Chaput, and Peter Todd Katzmarzyk published this 2016 study with the ISCOLE research group. It appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. It checks how many children meet Canada's twenty-four-hour movement guidelines. The guidelines combine nine to eleven hours of sleep, limited screen time, and daily active play. Data came from over six thousand children aged nine to eleven in twelve countries.

Sleep and activity were measured with accelerometers, while screen time came from self-reports. Children meeting all three recommendations had much lower odds of obesity than those meeting none. Meeting the guidelines was also linked to lower body mass index scores. Whenever daily activity was among the recommendations met, obesity odds dropped further. The results support treating sleep, screens, and exercise as one daily package for child health.
openalex-w2895074862:
Jisen Zhang, Xingtan Zhang, and Haibao Tang lead a global team sequencing a wild sugarcane in Nature Genetics in 2018. Cultivated sugarcanes are hybrids between species, with unusually complex genomes. Modern varieties carry about eighty percent chromosomes from sweet Saccharum officinarum. The rest comes from Saccharum spontaneum, a sugar-poor wild relative bred in for hardiness and disease resistance.

Because sugarcane is an autopolyploid, each gene exists in several similar copies. Sorting out which DNA belongs to which allele copy had blocked a true reference genome. This paper delivers an allele-defined genome for S. spontaneum itself. Resolving alleles separately exposes variation that merged assemblies hide. Breeders gain a map of the wild traits, stress tolerance and ratooning vigor, that modern canes borrowed. The genome opens focused improvement of one of the world's great sugar and biofuel crops.
openalex-w3093432062:
Pierre Friedlingstein, Michael O'Sullivan, Matthew Jones, and colleagues published the Global Carbon Budget 2020 in Earth System Science Data. The report tracks how much carbon dioxide humans emit and where it goes. Getting that budget right underpins climate policy and forecasts of future warming.

The team synthesizes datasets and methods for the budget's five major parts: fossil emissions, land use change, and the shares absorbed by air, ocean, and land. Each part carries stated uncertainty. Fossil emissions rest on energy statistics, while the natural sinks rest on models and observations. Issued yearly by a large international team, the budget is the reference ledger against which climate pledges are judged.
openalex-w4386220262:
Medha Barbhaiya, Stéphane Zuily, Ray Naden, and colleagues present the 2023 classification criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome, in the Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. The syndrome, shortened to APS, makes blood clot too readily and complicates pregnancy. Classification criteria define who counts as having APS in studies and trials. The American College of Rheumatology and EULAR backed this joint effort to sharpen them.

The team built the criteria in four phases, from literature review and surveys to expert voting and validation. Patients enter the scheme only with a positive antibody test close in time to a relevant symptom. Weighted points then accrue across six clinical and two laboratory domains. Reaching set scores in both sides classifies a patient as having APS for research.
openalex-w4386833262:
Israel Borges do Nascimento, Hebatullah Abdulazeem, Lenny Vasanthan, and colleagues review what helps or blocks health workers using digital tools. Their review appeared in npj Digital Medicine in 2023. Digital health covers wearables, decision support software, and telemedicine. Such tools can cut costs, raise care quality, and leave staff more satisfied. Use is already high for records and telemedicine in many places, yet uneven.

Adoption varies with ethnicity, location, age, and specialty, the authors note, revealing a digital divide. Barriers arise when tools are created, rolled out, and used day to day. Pulling the evidence together shows managers where training, design, or infrastructure fails. It also shows which supports actually get technology into routine practice.
openalex-w4390175962:
Debora Weber-Wulff, Alla Anohina-Naumeca, Sonja Bjelobaba, and colleagues tested tools that claim to detect AI-written text. Their study appeared in the International Journal for Educational Integrity in 2023. New language models made machine text easy to produce, and schools rushed to find detectors. The team asked whether the tools can reliably tell human writing from ChatGPT output. They also tested whether translation or deliberate disguise fools the detectors.

Fourteen systems were examined, twelve public tools plus two commercial ones used widely in education. The verdict was blunt: the tools are neither accurate nor reliable. They lean toward calling text human-written, missing much machine output. Disguise techniques made performance far worse. The authors warn against punishing students on such shaky evidence.
openalex-w7152395362: Safety checklists only work if nurses actually follow them. This study translated the Compliance with Standard Precautions Scale into Japanese and validated it among Japanese nurses. The authors ran a two-phase adaptation. A nursing-research study of measuring safety culture across languages.
openalex-w7204261862: When a woman is murdered, her children become orphans of femicide, and the state owes them care. This paper studies whether Brazil's support networks actually reach these indirect victims. The authors measure the gap between legal promises of full protection and what families receive. A somber legal study of children left behind by gender violence.
openalex-w7204263062: The Red Pill ideology, an online worldview hostile to women, is spreading in Brazil. This study maps the country's academic research on the movement and its ties to gender violence. The authors survey the literature to chart what scholars know so far. A timely mapping of a digital subculture with real-world harms.
openalex-w7204271762: Heavy bleeding after birth remains a top killer of mothers worldwide. This narrative review covers how to recognize postpartum hemorrhage fast, manage it with a team, and improve outcomes. The authors synthesize current best practice for obstetric emergencies. A clinical review where the message is clear: readiness saves mothers.
openalex-w7212064162:
Joice Aline de Sa and Janaina Guimaraes Mansilia study heat at work, and the rules that guard those who labor in it. Their focus is a recent change to Brazil's safety rules on heat exposure. Outdoor trades bear the brunt: farm work and building work above all. The pair read the new rules, the labor law, and past work on health in hot jobs.

Illness from sun and heat has risen, they note, from sunstroke to loss of body water. Looser rules, they argue, would roll back rights that workers have won. That roll-back would clash with a guard in law against such loss. Pay for harsh work also sits in the debate. The authors close with a call: tighten the guard for outdoor work, and press both state and bosses to act first.
openalex-w7213463062:
Manuela Xavier Borges leads a student outreach project on basic sanitation in Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro. Their 2026 report concerns the Parque Esperança neighbourhood and pupils in the later years of elementary school. Medical students ran the activity, linking dirty water and dumped waste to disease spread.

Sessions combined a talk, a diagnostic quiz, and making home water filters from plastic bottles. After the activity, pupils answered every final question correctly, the team reports. That result is presented as evidence of effective learning. Beyond facts, the project aimed at critical awareness and social responsibility. It shows university students teaching health and environment topics in a hands-on, low-cost format.
openalex-w7213537262: Big blasts send pressure waves circling the globe. This paper modeled eruption-born wave types in a layered air model, testing how winds bend them. The team figured loudness and travel times. An air-physics study of the planet ringing like a bell.
openalex-w7213596462: ICU scores and patient suffering do not always agree. This study compared clinical risk scores like qSOFA and NEWS2 against how septic shock patients themselves rated their symptoms. The authors probed the gap. A critical-care study of numbers versus lived experience.
openalex-w7214239262:
Murilo Vinícius Vieira Siqueira and Jeferson Freitas Toregeani compared two ways to restore blood flow in badly blocked leg arteries in a 2026 retrospective study. One group of patients had open surgery; the other had a less invasive procedure done through the vessels. The team followed 140 patients treated at one center between 2015 and 2025.

Clinical outcomes and limb salvage were similar in both groups, with no clear statistical gap. Rates of major adverse limb events and major amputation also matched. What predicted failure was not the technique but the patient: worse ischemia at arrival and diabetes stood out. The findings suggest doctors should weigh the patient's overall condition at least as heavily as the procedure they choose.
openalex-w7214323962:
